lead: Best-effort delivery gives every packet the same treatment: no promise of bandwidth, no limit on delay. Quality of service (QoS) turns that into a contract. Packets are classified into flows, shaped to a rate, queued per flow and scheduled so each flow gets its promised share. Integrated Services goes further and reserves resources for a flow end to end, using RSVP to carry the request and admission control to accept or reject it. You meet this whenever a voice call must not wait behind a file download — a UPI payment, a hospital monitor, a live cricket stream.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.6 for why TCP alone cannot promise delay, and the queueing basics from Unit 3, Data Link Layer and Medium Access.

sections.h3: The four parameters of quality of service

blocks.text: QoS is described by four parameters. Reliability is how much data is lost — the fraction of packets that never arrive. Delay is the time a packet takes from source to destination, in milliseconds. Jitter is the variation in that delay: if packet 1 takes 20 ms and packet 2 takes 55 ms, the jitter is 35 ms. Bandwidth is the rate the flow needs, in bits per second.

Different applications care about different parameters. A file transfer needs reliability and bandwidth and can wait seconds. A voice call needs low delay (under about 150 ms one way), low jitter and only about 64 kbps, but tolerates a little loss. Video needs bandwidth and jitter control. A stock ticker needs reliability and delay together.

Plain IP gives best effort: first come, first served, no guarantee for anyone. Adding bandwidth does not fix jitter, because a bigger pipe still lets one large packet push a small one aside at a router. QoS is the set of mechanisms that fixes this deliberately, by classifying packets and treating classes differently.

sections.h3: Scheduling and shaping inside a router

blocks.text: A router with QoS classifies each packet into a flow, polices the flow's rate, queues it, and schedules it. Scheduling decides which queued packet leaves next.

items: FIFO (first in, first out): one queue, arrival order, no QoS.
Priority queueing: several queues with priorities; the highest non-empty priority always wins. Strict priority can starve low-priority traffic.

Weighted fair queueing (WFQ): every flow gets its own queue and is served in proportion to a weight wᵢ. Flow i gets roughly wᵢ ÷ Σwⱼ of the link rate. With weights 1, 1, 2 on a 4 Mbps link, the third flow gets 2 Mbps and the other two get 1 Mbps each.

blocks.text: Shaping delays excess packets; policing drops or marks them. The leaky bucket drains at a constant rate r, so its output rate never exceeds r whatever the input burst — bursty traffic becomes a smooth stream. The token bucket stores tokens that arrive at rate r, up to a depth b, and a packet of L bits leaves only if L tokens are present.

blocks.where: b is the bucket depth in bits (the largest burst allowed at once); r is the token rate in bits per second (the long-run average); t is the elapsed time in seconds, starting with a full bucket.

blocks.text: So a token bucket limits the average rate and permits a burst of b bits; a leaky bucket permits no burst at all.

Integrated Services (IntServ) makes a reservation before sending. Each flow is described by a TSpec (traffic specification), five numbers: token bucket rate r, token bucket depth b, peak rate p, minimum policed unit m, and maximum packet size M. This book writes r and p in bits per second and b in bits. The standard TSpec (RFC 2210) defines r, b, p, m and M all in bytes, with r and p in bytes per second. Convert before comparing with link rates.

The sender states a service class and its TSpec. RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol) carries the request hop by hop to every router on the path. Each router runs admission control: it adds the new TSpec to what is already promised and checks whether link capacity and queue budget still suffice. If yes, the flow is admitted and resources are committed; if no, the request is rejected and the sender is told. Existing flows keep their promises either way — that is the whole point.

Two classes exist. Guaranteed service promises a firm upper bound on queueing delay for a flow that stays inside its TSpec. Controlled load promises only that the flow will see a lightly loaded network — very low loss and delay, but no firm number.

The scaling problem: a core router may carry millions of flows, and per-flow state plus a reservation message per flow does not fit. DiffServ answers this by marking each packet with a DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) in the IP header and giving per-class, not per-flow, treatment.

figure.caption: Admission control runs once at reservation setup: RSVP brings the TSpec, and the router admits or rejects the flow. After admission, every packet takes the per-packet path: classify, police with a token bucket, queue per flow for weighted fair queueing, then leave under guaranteed or controlled-load service.

spec.title: What a reserved flow passes through

nodes.label: Admission control
nodes.note: once per flow: admit or reject

spec.aria: A flow diagram in which RSVP brings a TSpec to admission control once per flow, which admits or rejects it. After admission each packet is classified into a flow, is policed by a token bucket, waits in a per-flow queue served by weighted fair queueing, and leaves under guaranteed or controlled-load service.

examples.question: A token bucket at a router's ingress has depth b = 16 000 bits and token rate r = 2 Mbps. The bucket is full at t = 0 and the flow always has data ready. (a) How many bits can the flow send in the first 4 s? (b) What is the largest burst it can hand over at t = 0?
steps: Write the data with units: r = 2 Mbps = 2 × 10⁶ bits/s, b = 16 000 bits, t = 4 s.
Part (b) first. At t = 0 the bucket holds b tokens, and a packet of L bits needs L tokens. So the largest instantaneous burst is b = 16 000 bits = 16 000 ÷ 8 = 2000 bytes.
Part (a). Tokens earned in 4 s: r × t = 2 × 10⁶ × 4 = 8 000 000 bits.
Add the tokens already in the bucket: b + r × t = 16 000 + 8 000 000 = 8 016 000 bits.
Check against a plain 2 Mbps limiter: it would allow 8 000 000 bits in 4 s. The token bucket allows 16 000 bits more — exactly the saved burst.
examples.answer: In the first 4 s the flow can send 8 016 000 bits (about 1 MB), and the largest burst at t = 0 is 16 000 bits, that is 2000 bytes.
examples.check:
b = 16000
r = 2 * 10**6
t = 4
total = b + r * t
burst = b
print(total)
print(burst)

traps: Treating a token bucket as a peak-rate limiter. It limits the long-run average to r and lets a burst of b bits through; only a leaky bucket forces a flat output rate.
Mixing up IntServ (per-flow reservation, RSVP, admission control, per-flow state) with DiffServ (per-class DSCP marking, no per-flow state).

Mixing bits and bytes when converting TSpec values. The standard TSpec defines r, b, p, m and M all in bytes (r and p in bytes per second); this book writes rates in bits per second. Convert before comparing with link rates.
Swapping shaping and policing: shaping delays excess traffic, policing drops or marks it.
Forgetting that admission control exists to protect flows already admitted, not to help the new one.

quiz.q: Name the four QoS parameters and give the unit of each.
quiz.a: Reliability (fraction of packets lost, no unit), delay (milliseconds), jitter (milliseconds, the variation in delay) and bandwidth (bits per second).

quiz.q: Why does upgrading a link from 10 Mbps to 100 Mbps not remove jitter?
quiz.a: Jitter comes from queueing delay varying: a voice packet may find the queue empty one moment and behind a large data packet the next. A faster link shortens each wait but does not stop the queue depth from varying, so delay still varies unless scheduling gives each flow its own queue and a guaranteed share.

quiz.q: A 10 Mbps link uses weighted fair queueing with three flows of weights 1, 1 and 2. What rate does each flow get?
quiz.a: Sum of weights = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. Flow 1: (1/4) × 10 = 2.5 Mbps. Flow 2: 2.5 Mbps. Flow 3: (2/4) × 10 = 5 Mbps.

quiz.q: A token bucket has r = 1 Mbps and b = 8000 bits, full at t = 0. How many bits can the flow send in the first 2 s?
A router already carries flows whose TSpecs add up to 90% of a 100 Mbps link. A new flow asks for 15 Mbps. What does admission control decide, and why is that good for the existing flows?
quiz.a: 90 + 15 = 105 Mbps > 100 Mbps, so the request is rejected. Accepting it would make every flow miss its promised delay and bandwidth, so rejecting the newcomer keeps the existing guarantees true.

quiz.q: Why does DiffServ scale better than IntServ in the core of the Internet?
quiz.a: IntServ keeps state and runs a reservation per flow, so an edge router or core router with millions of flows must store and process millions of records. DiffServ keeps no per-flow state: it sets a DSCP in the IP header and each router applies one of a few per-class behaviours, so the work per packet is constant however many flows pass through.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, operators build QoS with Linux tc (htb for weighted fair queueing, tbf for token bucket), and RSVP still appears as RSVP-TE inside MPLS for traffic engineering. Mobile networks express the same idea as 5G QoS flows, each with a 5QI value that fixes delay and loss targets. DiffServ's expedited forwarding and assured forwarding classes are what carry voice in many carrier backbones. Search next for "DiffServ assured forwarding", "RSVP-TE" and "5G QoS flow 5QI" if you want to see the reservation idea deployed.
